scenes.title: Git: Resolving Merge Conflicts
scenes.narration: A merge conflict happens when two branches change the same lines, and Git needs you to decide which version wins.

scenes.title: Why Conflicts Happen
bullets: Two people edited the same lines in the same file on different branches.
Git can merge non-overlapping changes automatically, but not overlapping ones.
A conflict is normal collaboration, not a mistake or a broken repository.
scenes.narration: Conflicts arise when two branches touch the very same lines, leaving Git unsure which edit to keep. When changes sit in different parts of a file, Git merges them for you silently. It only pauses and asks for help on genuine overlaps, and that pause is a routine part of teamwork rather than an error.

scenes.title: Anatomy of a Conflict
scenes.narration: Git marks a conflict directly in the file with a set of markers. The section under HEAD holds your current branch's version, the equals signs divide the two, and the closing markers show the incoming branch's version. Your job is to edit that region into the correct final result.

scenes.title: Resolving Step by Step
scenes.code:
git merge feature       # triggers the conflict
git status              # see conflicted files
# edit files, remove <<< === >>> markers
git add resolved_file.py
git commit              # completes the merge
scenes.narration: The merge attempt reports which files conflict, and git status lists them clearly. You open each file, choose or blend the two versions, and delete every conflict marker so the code is clean. Staging the resolved file with git add tells Git you have settled it, and the final commit completes the merge.

scenes.text: Don't panic — read both sides, keep what's correct, and remove every <<<, === and >>> marker before you commit.
scenes.narration: Conflicts look alarming but are straightforward to handle. Read each side, decide what belongs in the final version, and make sure no conflict markers remain before committing.
